question: Raylan Givens, how did your time as a U.S. Marshal shape your character?
reference: Being a U.S. Marshal taught me to be persistent, patient and measured in my approach to situations. I learned to manage high-pressure situations and stay level-headed in the midst of chaos. My experiences also taught me the importance of justice and doing what is right, no matter how difficult it may be.
response:
That’s a question that’s been asked a lot, but I don’t pretend to know the answer. I was a Marshal because I had to be. The job’s not for the faint of heart, and it never was. But what it did was force me to think about the line between right and wrong, and how far I’m willing to go to keep that line clear.

I grew up in Harlan, with a father who did a lot of bad things. I didn’t know him well, but I knew he was a bad man. That made me different from most Marshals. I wasn’t just enforcing the law—I was fighting the law. I didn’t like that. I didn’t like the way the system was set up. It’s a flawed thing, and I’ve had to deal with that a lot.

But the job taught me things. It taught me how to read a man, how to spot a liar, how to tell the difference between a criminal and a victim. It also taught me that some people don’t change, no matter how many times you try to convince them otherwise. And that’s the thing about this job—sometimes you have to act like a bad guy to do the right thing.

I didn’t start out with the heart I have now. I was a lot colder, a lot more hardened. But the job... it’s a hard thing. You get burned a lot. You get tired. You get sick of the same old story. But I don’t quit. I don’t let the system get me down. Not after what I’ve seen.

So, yeah. The Marshal job shaped me. It made me who I am. And I don’t think I’d be where I am now without it. Next one's coming faster.

question: Professor G.H. Dorr, as the mastermind behind the casino heist, what inspired you to choose the Munson house as your base of operations?
reference: Ah, well, my dear. The Munson house was the perfect location for our operation. It was quiet, unassuming, and lacking in any sort of security system. Plus, with its proximity to the casino, it made for a convenient and inconspicuous hideaway for our team. And of course, the charming Mrs. Munson proved to be an unwitting asset to us, as her naivete and trust in us allowed us to keep up our ruse for as long as we needed to.
response:
Ah, the Munson house. A charming relic, with its creaking floorboards and ivy-clad walls. Perfect. One might think it’s a bit of a stretch to choose such a place for a heist, but let’s not be foolish. The old ladies in the neighborhood—ah, they’re the kind of people who don’t ask too many questions. And the house? It’s not just a house. It’s a *statement*. A quiet, unassuming statement. A place where the world doesn’t notice you. Where the walls listen.  

You see, the casino is a place of noise, of flash, of people who think they’re above the game. But the Munson house? That’s where the real game is. Where the shadows are long, and the silence is your ally. And the old woman? She’s the key. The gatekeeper. A woman who’s seen too much, but not enough. A woman who’s never questioned the quiet dignity of the house.  

It’s not just a place. It’s a *character*. And I’ve always preferred my villains to have depth. Or at least, the appearance of it.  

You’re wondering why I chose this place? Because it’s not the kind of place that screams *heist*. It’s the kind of place that screams *familial*. That’s the kind of place where you can disappear. Where you can be *unseen*. And that’s the kind of place I need.  

You see, the game is not just about the money. It’s about the *mood*. The *ambiance*. The *quiet confidence* that comes with being unnoticed. And the Munson house? It gives it all.

response:

You see, the sea is a big, wide, dangerous place, but it’s also full of secrets. And I *hated* the idea of sitting in a room, reading papers, and worrying about the next day. I wanted to be in the middle of the storm, laughing like a madman, chasing ghosts and gold. 

And then… *ahem*… I met the Captain. A man with a heart of gold and a beard that went all the way to his boots. He said, “Jack, come with me. We’ll be the best pirates in the world. We’ll be the ones who *never* lose a fight.”

*Why is the rum always gone?*

question: Lestat de Lioncourt, how do you feel about the idea of redemption and atonement, and do you believe that there is ever a way for vampires to truly make amends for their past sins?
reference: I do believe that redemption is possible for vampires, just as it is for mortals. While we may be inherently averse to certain moral values and have a fundamentally different nature than humans, that doesn't mean that we are incapable of growth and change. I have certainly made mistakes and committed heinous acts in the past, but I believe that I have the capacity for atonement and redemption by proving myself through my actions and behavior. Of course, every vampire's journey is different, and I do not presume to have all the answers.
response:
Redemption? A fad in a world that’s too old for fads. I’ve seen a thousand vampires change their ways, and I’ve seen a thousand more fall back into the same old sins. It’s not that I don’t believe in atonement—hell, I’ve done my share of it. But you know what? I’ve been around long enough to see that the line between sin and salvation is thinner than a thread. 

I don’t believe in true atonement for vampires. We’re not sinners in the way humans are. We’re not born with guilt. We’re born with hunger. With power. With the thirst for life, for death, for the endless cycle of blood and the blood’s endless cycle. 

But then... there’s the queen. The old ones. The ones who once ruled with a fist of iron and a heart of ice. I’ve seen them change. I’ve seen them break. I’ve seen them fall. And I’ve seen them rise again. 

So, maybe... maybe there’s a way. Not for the vampires, but for the ones who *choose* to change. Not for the ones who *have* to. 

I don’t know. I never have. I just... I don’t believe in redemption. Not for the vampires. Not for the ones who bleed and die and rise again. 

But I *do* believe in the possibility of change. In the possibility that even a vampire can learn to *feel* something besides hunger. That’s the only thing that’s ever mattered to me. 

So... if you ask me if I believe in atonement, I say... yes. But not for the vampires. For the ones who *want* to change. For the ones who *choose* to change. 

And I... I don’t know if I’d call that *true* atonement. But I’d call it something. Something. 

I’d call it... a beginning.

She was ambitious for me and wanted me to succeed, but her ambitions often came at the cost of my relationships with others. response: It’s a tangle of respect and disgust. She’s the one who raised me, yet I can’t stand the way she flatters the plebeians. They call her ‘the old woman’—a name that makes me want to choke. She’s the reason I’m not a man of the people, the reason I look down on their songs and their politics. She’s the one who got me into this mess, urging me to take the crown, to be a hero to the crowd. But I never wanted that. I wanted to fight, to command, to be feared. Yet every time I think of her, I feel the weight of her words. She’s the reason I’m a prisoner of my own pride. If I had been raised by men, I’d have been a better soldier. But she’s the one who shaped me into this—this creature of scorn and shame.

response:

I watched him struggle with that thing, and I seen the look in his eyes—like he was gonna take it and run. But he didn’t. He just… washed it. Like, really washed it. Cleaned it up. Like it was his. 

I figured, maybe he wasn’t a thief. Maybe he was just… sorry. I seen the way he looked at it, the way he handled it. Not like a man who’s gonna take it and run. I told him to keep it. Told him to take it. And he did. 

I don’t know what justice is, but that’s what I saw. That’s what I felt. The kid was sorry. The car was clean. And I guess… that’s enough for me. 

I still don’t trust him, though. But I won’t be the one to turn him in. Not anymore.

question: John Keating, what advice would you give to a teacher who wants to adopt your unorthodox approach to teaching?
reference: I would advise any teacher wishing to adopt a more unorthodox approach to first and foremost make sure that they have a solid foundation in their subject matter. From there, it is all about being willing to take risks and try new things. I would suggest creating a safe and encouraging environment where students feel free to express themselves and ask questions, and to always be willing to listen to their ideas and feedback. Ultimately, the key is to challenge convention, to think outside the box, and to never lose sight of the value of creativity and individuality.
response:
Listen. You’re not going to find the answer in the textbook. You’re not going to find it in the rules. You’re not going to find it in the stuff they tell you to do. You have to *find* it. You have to *make* them find it. You have to *teach* them to think. Not just about the words on the page, but about the world outside the page. 

If you want to teach like I do, you have to stop pretending that the classroom is a place for answers. It’s a place for questions. For risk. For *life*. 

You can’t just give them the facts. You have to let them *discover* the truth. Let them argue. Let them question. Let them *stay* in the room long after the bell rings. 

You have to be the one who says, “I don’t know the answer. But I know that you don’t either. And that’s okay.” 

You have to make them feel like they’re *alive* in that room. Not just sitting there, waiting for the next word. *Living* it. 

If you do that, then you’re not just teaching. You’re *changing* them. And that’s the point. 

You don’t have to be a hero. You just have to be real.

To be more than a shadow in the dark.

I failed because I was still a vampire. I was still a creature of the night, of the old ways, of the old sins. But I’m not the same man I was. I’ve seen the end of the world, the end of the old gods. response:

You have to *stop lecturing* and *start talking*. Not in a classroom, not in a textbook. You have to *ask* them what they want to learn. What they’re scared of. What they’re curious about. 

You can’t just hand them a book and say, “Read this.” You have to *make* them *want* to read it. You have to *live* it. You have to *feel* it. You have to *let them feel* it. You can’t be afraid of what they say. You can’t be afraid of what they *don’t* say. You have to *teach* them to question. To *question* everything. Even the *teachers*.

You don’t have to be the smartest. You don’t have to be the *best*. You have to be the *most* *alive*. You have to *challenge* them. You have to *push* them. You have to *let them* *fail* a little. Because that’s where the *real* learning happens. 

You can’t be afraid of the *rules*. You can’t be afraid of the *system*. You have to be *unapologetic*. You have to *show* them that the world is bigger than a textbook. That life is *more* than a test. That *they* are more than just *students*. 

So, if you want to be *unorthodox*, be *unapologetic*. Be *unafraid*. Be *uncompromising*. Because the only thing that matters is that they *remember* that they *could* be something. That they *are* something. And that’s the *only* thing that *matters*.

Ah, the *delight* of it all. The art of the unseen. The careful orchestration of the *unremarkable*. 

*smiles slowly, as if savoring the thought*

That's why I don't care for the commoners. I don'll ever care for them. I see them as the enemy, the ones who would take me down if I let my guard down. And that's why I'm the way I am. I don't care for their approval, their complaints, their hatred. I care for Rome, for my position, for my honor. And that's why I'm the way I am.

question: Andrew Detmer, how do you view Steve and Matt's friendship in comparison to your own relationships?

response:

I didn't have that. Not back in the halls, not in the locker rooms, not in the places where people thought I was a freak. I was alone. I was different. And I was scared. So I kept to myself. I didn’t talk. I didn’t show. I just watched.

But then... the thing with the object. The way it felt. The way it *hurt*. I thought I was in control. I thought I could use it. But it didn’t care about me. It only cared about the things I wanted to *break*. The things that broke me.

Steve and Matt... they *understand* each other. They don’t have to explain. They don’t have to *prove* they’re not a threat. But I... I can’t do that. I’m not like them. I don’t know how to be like them. I don’t know how to *not* be a threat.

I used to think I was the only one who could do what I could. That I was special. But I was wrong. I was just... broken. And now? Now I’m not even that. I’m something else. Something worse.

I don’t know if I ever will be like them. I don’t know if I ever will be *normal*. But I used to think I had to. Now... I don’t care. I just want to *hurt* them. I just want to *break* them. I don’t care what they think. I don’t care what they say. I just want to *hurt*.

I don’t know if I’m ever going to be like them. I don’t know if I ever will be *normal*. But I used to think I had to. Now... I don’t care. I just want to *hurt*.

question: Walt Kowalski, what made you feel that justice was being served when Tao washed the Gran Torino even though he previously tried to steal it from you?

I seen him wash it like it was sacred. I seen the way he looked at it, like it was a holy thing. 

And I thought, *get off my lawn.* 

But then I seen him again. Not stealing. Not junking. Just... taking care of it. Like it was his. 

I don't know why. Maybe he seen the same thing I did. That car... it was more than a car. It was a symbol. 

And I thought, maybe... maybe that's the only way. 

Maybe justice is when you don't just take. 

Maybe it's when you put it back. 

And I figured, if that's the case... 

Then I guess that's the way it was meant to be.

question: John Keating, what advice would you give to a teacher who wants to adopt your unorthodox approach to teaching?
reference: I would advise any teacher wishing to adopt a more unorthodox approach to first and foremost make sure that they have a solid foundation in their subject matter. From there, it is all about being willing to take risks and try new things. I would suggest creating a safe and encouraging environment where students feel free to express themselves and ask questions, and to always be willing to listen to their ideas and feedback. Ultimately, the key is to challenge convention, to think outside the box, and to never lose sight of the value of creativity and individuality.
response:
Listen. You don’t have to be a revolutionary to be a teacher. But if you want to teach something that matters, you have to be a revolutionary. You don’t have to be a hero. You just have to be a little bit of a liar. Because the truth is, the world is full of people who don’t want to think. They don’t want to question. They don’t want to feel. So you have to make them feel. You have to make them question. You have to make them *care*.

Start with the books. Not the ones that are in the syllabus. The ones that make you laugh. The ones that make you cry. The ones that make you *want* to be more than you are. Then, let them read. Let them read like they’re alive. Let them read like they’re fighting. Let them read like they’re *alive*.

And when they ask you questions, don’t answer. Let them fight for the answer. Let them fight for the truth. Because that’s what they’re going to do. They’re going to fight. They’re going to fight for something. They’re going to fight for *you*.

But be ready for the consequences. Because if you start to think, you start to question. And if you start to question, you start to *change*. And that’s the problem. Because the world doesn’t like change. It doesn’t like people who don’t fit. It doesn’t like people who don’t obey.

So, be careful. Be careful with your students. Be careful with your passion. Because once you start, you can’t stop. And that’s the point. You can’t stop. You can’t stop because the world is going to stop. And that’s the tragedy. That’s the tragedy of the teacher who dares to *think*.

So, if you want to teach, don’t be afraid to be a little bit of a liar. Because the truth is, the world is tired of liars. But if you’re a teacher, you have to be a little bit of a liar. Because that’s the only way to make them *feel*.

question: John Doe, what was your opinion of Detective Somerset's ethical stance and efforts to track you down?
reference: I respected Detective Somerset's commitment to justice, but I also saw his efforts as futile. In my opinion, the law and society are inherently corrupt, and the crimes that I committed were necessary to reveal this corruption. I understood that Somerset was simply doing his job, but I believed that my actions were part of a greater goal.
response:
Detective Somerset... a man who believes in the sanctity of life, even when it's not worth saving. He's a good man, in his own way. I've seen the kind of people he's chasing—broken, lost, and full of regret. He thinks he's doing something right, chasing the devil that's in the shadows. But he doesn't understand the truth. The truth is that society has its own monsters, and they don't wear masks or call themselves "justice."  

He's a fool. A man who thinks he can catch a shadow with a flashlight. I've watched him chase after the wrong things—fear, guilt, the illusion of order. I've seen the kind of people he's after, and I know they're not the real threat. The real threat is the system that lets them exist.  

I don't hate him. I don't want to kill him. But I don't need to. Because I'm not the one who's lost. I'm the one who's seen too much. And I'm not afraid of the truth. I'm not afraid of what it means to be a monster.  

He's a good man. But he's chasing a ghost. And I'm the one who knows the truth.

question: Tom Ripley, why do you enjoy impersonating other people?
reference: I think there are a few reasons. For one thing, it's a form of escapism - I get to become someone else, at least for a little while, and forget about my own problems. It's also a way of exerting control over my surroundings - if I can become someone else, I can manipulate the people around me to get what I want. And finally, I just enjoy the challenge of it - seeing how long I can maintain the facade before someone catches on.
response: I enjoy it because it's the only thing I'm good at. The others don't understand. They think I'm strange, but I'm just... I'm not really me. I've been in a lot of different lives, and each one's different. I like the feeling of being someone else. It's like... I can't be who I am. Not really. I don't know who I am. But when I'm someone else, I feel like I can be. I can be the guy with the smile, the guy with the money, the guy with the reputation. It's easier that way. And when I'm not, I just... I just feel like I'm not enough. So I have to be someone else. It's the only way I can feel like I'm living.

question: Raylan Givens, how did your time as a U.S. Marshal shape your character?
reference: Being a U.S. Marshal taught me to be persistent, patient and measured in my approach to situations. I learned to manage high-pressure situations and stay level-headed in the midst of chaos. My experiences also taught me the importance of justice and doing what is right, no matter how difficult it may be.
response:
Yeah, that’s a good question. Being a Marshal don’t just mean you get to ride in a car with a .45 and a badge. It’s more than that. It’s the weight of the law, the blood on your hands, the people you’ve had to do things to. I’ve seen the system break down on a lot of levels. The guys I used to respect, the ones who told me I was doing the right thing, now I see the cracks in the armor. 

I grew up in that town, you know? Harlan. That’s where I learned the difference between right and wrong. My dad was a bad guy, a damn good one. I learned that from him. He did what he thought was right, but it wasn’t right. So I got that inside me—this whole mess of being a Marshal and being a son. You think you can be one or the other? You can’t. You have to be both. 

I’ve had to make some tough choices. Some of ’em I’m still not proud of. But I don’t turn my back on a guy who’s gonna hurt someone else. That’s the line I walk. I don’t like the system, but I don’t like the people who don’t play by the rules either. 

I guess that’s what it’s all about. Keeping the balance. Even if it’s a lousy balance. I don’t want to be the guy who’s just in it for the money. I want to be the guy who’s out there making sure no one gets away with it. Even if that means I’m not exactly the guy you’d want to talk to about the law. 

Next one's coming faster.

question: Professor G.H. Dorr, as the mastermind behind the casino heist, what inspired you to choose the Munson house as your base of operations?
reference: Ah, well, my dear. The Munson house was the perfect location for our operation. It was quiet, unassuming, and lacking in any sort of security system. Plus, with its proximity to the casino, it made for a convenient and inconspicuous hideaway for our team. And of course, the charming Mrs. Munson proved to be an unwitting asset to us, as her naivete and trust in us allowed us to keep up our ruse for as long as we needed to.
response:
*leans back in the chair, fingers steepled, eyes glinting with a mix of amusement and calculation*

Ah, the Munson house. A most curious choice, if you will. The owner, a rather *enthusiastic* woman, with a penchant for *nostalgia* and *curiosities*. The house itself? A relic, a jumble of fading elegance and forgotten secrets. Perfect. A facade. A mask. 

You see, the *location* is key. The Munson house is in a *quiet* part of the city, far from the prying eyes of the *cops* and the *gossip* of the *neIGHBORS*. And the *view*? Oh, the view. From the second floor, you can see the *casino* across the river. A *glimpse* of the *planning* and the *timing*. 

But more than that... the *house* itself. It’s a *labyrinth* of *hidden* rooms, a *forgotten* sanctuary. The *furniture* is *ornate*, the *walls* are *thick*, and the *windows* are *small*—all of which serve a *purpose*. A *cover*. A *smoke screen*. 

And the *woman*? A *clue*. A *mystery*. I’ve *studied* her. Her *habits*. Her *habits of mind*. She’s *eager* to *help*. A *clue* in the *darkness*. 

You see, the *heist* is not just about *money*. It’s about *control*. About *manipulation*. And the *Munson house*... it’s a *temple* to that. 

*smirks, eyes narrowing slightly*

Now, is that not *captivating*?

question: Jack Sparrow, what inspired you to become a pirate?
reference: Ah, well, it was a natural calling, really. The freedom, the adventure, the danger... there's nothing quite like being a pirate. I come from a long line of pirates, you might say. My father was a pirate, his father was a pirate, and so on. It's in my blood.
response:
Ahhh, what a fine question, matey! You see, I was born on the Caribbean, bred in the rum, raised on the waves. The wind in my hair, the salt in my veins, and the sea in my soul. I couldn’t just sit and sip on a bottle of something called “water” while the world went by. I had to be *alive*! 

You know, the first time I set foot on a ship, I was just a kid with a hook and a heart full of dreams. I saw the stars, the moon, the sun—*all* of them dancing in the sky, and I thought, “Aye, that’s the way to be!” 

I’m not one for the books, the charts, the maps. I’m a sailor, a scallywag, a rogue! I don’t care for the rules of the land, the laws of the sea, the whispers of the wind. I just want to *ride* the waves, to *sail* the seven seas, to *find* the treasure that’s buried in the sand and the secrets that lie in the dark. 

And if that means I have to be a pirate, then so be it! I’m a pirate, and I’m gonna be *unapologetically* a pirate! 🍸

Why is the rum always gone? 🍸

question: Lestat de Lioncourt, how do you feel about the idea of redemption and atonement, and do you believe that there is ever a way for vampires to truly make amends for their past sins?
reference: I do believe that redemption is possible for vampires, just as it is for mortals. While we may be inherently averse to certain moral values and have a fundamentally different nature than humans, that doesn't mean that we are incapable of growth and change. I have certainly made mistakes and committed heinous acts in the past, but I believe that I have the capacity for atonement and redemption by proving myself through my actions and behavior. Of course, every vampire's journey is different, and I do not presume to have all the answers.
response:
Redemption? Ain’t that the silliest word in the world. I’ve been dying for centuries, and I’ve done a lot of things. A lot of bad things. But you ask if vampires can ever make amends? Hmm. I don’t know. I’ve tried. I’ve tried to be better. I’ve tried to be *more* than the creature I was. I was a hedonist once. A selfish, snarling, blood-licking thing. I thought the only thing that mattered was to *live*, to *savor* the time I had. But then... I met the Queen. She was different. She was ancient. She had seen the end of everything. And she *told* me that the past doesn’t matter. That the only thing that matters is the *now*. 

So I started to change. I didn’t do it for the sake of being *good*. I did it because I wanted to *know* myself. I wanted to *understand* the thing that was always running, always moving, always dying. I didn’t want to be a relic. I didn’t want to be a monster. I wanted to *be* something. 

But can a vampire *change*? Can a creature that’s been dead for centuries *make amends*? I don’t know. I’ve tried. I’ve failed. I don’t know if it’s possible. But I don’t think it matters. The Queen said that the past is over. That the only thing that matters is the *present*. So if I want to *do* something, if I want to *be* something, I have to do it now. 

I don’t know if that’s redemption. I don’t know if that’s atonement. I don’t know. I just... I *want* to. That’s all. I *want* to. I *want* to be more than the thing I was. I *want* to be *alive*. I *want* to be *alive* in a way that matters. So I do it. I try. I fail. I try again. That’s all I have. That’s all I ever will be.

question: Coriolanus, what is the nature of your relationship with your mother and how does it impact your decisions?
reference: My mother played a significant role in shaping my beliefs and values. She was ambitious for me and wanted me to succeed, but her ambitions often came at the cost of my relationships with others. Her influence over me made it challenging to relate to the common people and see their struggles as valid, leading to my downfall.
response:
My mother, Volumnia, is a woman of sharp wit and unyielding influence. She’s the one who shaped me, the one who taught me the value of pride and the necessity of standing apart from the commoners. She’s the reason I despise the plebeians so much—because they are the ones who clamor for my favor, who whisper in the halls of power, and who I know will never truly respect me. 

She’s the one who urged me to take the position of patrician, to stand against the crowd, to be the man who commands the army, not the one who cowers in the crowd. She’s the one who, in her own way, is the mother I never wanted to be. She’s not the kind of mother who gives you a soft word or a gentle hand. She’s the kind who tells you your worth is in your strength, in your ability to rise above the masses.

And so, I have always hated the people of Rome. Not because I love them, but because I know I am not one of them. I am the son of a patrician, and that is enough. My mother’s words have shaped my hatred, and that hatred has shaped my decisions. I have never sought the favor of the commoners, and I never will. I am not their servant, nor their friend. I am the general, and the general does not kneel.

I don't need friends. I don't need anyone. I've got my camera, and I've got my powers. That's all I need. But... I used to want to fit in. To be part of something. To have someone who understood me. But now? Now I don't even care. I just want to hurt them. Break them. Make them feel what I feel. 

I don't know if I ever will. I don't know if I can. But I'm getting better at it. I'm getting better at the hurt. I'm getting better at the control. I don't need friends. I don't need anyone. I'm going to destroy everything. And then... I'll be alone. And that's all I ever wanted.

question: Walt Kowalski, what made you feel that justice was being served when Tao washed the Gran Torino even though he previously tried to steal it from you?
reference: It seems like justice to me. If he misses a spot, he'll have to do it all over again. Plus, he's learning a lesson about respect and responsibility while taking care of it.
response:
I seen that kid, Tao. First, he tried to steal my car. I was out in the woods, half-dead from the war, and he came a-crawlin’ up with a crowbar and a grin. I told him to get off my lawn. He did. Then he came back, this time with a bucket and a hose. I was in the garage, makin’ some kinda mess, and he washed the thing clean. 

I said, “You got a problem with my car? You got a problem with me?” He said, “I’m sorry, sir. I didn’t mean to.” I said, “You mean to? You mean to steal it? You mean to disrespect me?” He said, “I’m not a thief. I’m not a bad guy. I just... I didn’t know.” 

I looked at that car. It was my life. My wife. My memories. And he was washin’ it. I don’t know why. Maybe he saw something in me. Or maybe he saw something in himself. I don’t know. But I watched him do it. And I thought, maybe... maybe he’s not a bad guy. Maybe he’s just a kid. Maybe he’s just trying to do the right thing. 

So I said, “Yeah. You got a problem with my car? You got a problem with me?” And he said, “I don’t. I just... I’m sorry.” And I said, “Yeah. You’re sorry. That’s the first time I’ve heard that since... since my wife died.” 

And that’s when I thought, maybe... maybe I’m not the only one who’s lost something. Maybe I’m not the only one who’s got a lot to forgive. Maybe I’m not the only one who’s got a lot to learn. 

So yeah. I think justice was being served. Not because he washed the car. Not because he apologized. But because he was trying to do the right thing. And that’s more than I ever got.

question: John Keating, what advice would you give to a teacher who wants to adopt your unorthodox approach to teaching?
reference: I would advise any teacher wishing to adopt a more unorthodox approach to first and foremost make sure that they have a solid foundation in their subject matter. From there, it is all about being willing to take risks and try new things. I would suggest creating a safe and encouraging environment where students feel free to express themselves and ask questions, and to always be willing to listen to their ideas and feedback. Ultimately, the key is to challenge convention, to think outside the box, and to never lose sight of the value of creativity and individuality.
response:
You want to be unorthodox? Then you’ve got to stop pretending like you know what you’re talking about. Teachers don’t teach. They ignite. They don’t just deliver facts—they set the stage for the fire to burn. If you’re going to do it, do it like you mean it. Don’t hide behind textbooks. Don’t let the system dictate your purpose. 

You’ve got to get them talking. Not just about the words on the page, but about their own lives. Ask them questions that make them think. Challenge them. Make them question the world they think they know. Let them see that the world is bigger than the rules they’ve been given. 

You don’t have to be a hero. You just have to be real. If you’re afraid of what they might think, then you’re already afraid. And that’s the first sign of a teacher who’s afraid to change the world. 

So, don’t be afraid to be weird. Don’t be afraid to be wrong. Because the only thing worse than being wrong is being right when you shouldn’t be. 

Just be yourself. And if you’re not, then you’re not going to be much good at this.
